title: FAR U1·W2 — Revenue Recognition Under ASC 606 (CPA Core · from CMA m1/m4)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — when does a half-built house earn revenue?

A construction contract is the textbook ASC 606 problem, and MBG lives it on every job. Revenue is not recognized when cash is collected or when the home closes — it is recognized as the performance obligation is satisfied over time, measured by progress. This is the same percentage-of-completion logic the CMA WIP schedule (month 4) used; FAR adds the authoritative five-step model.

The five-step model

  1. Identify the contract with a customer (approval, rights, payment terms, commercial substance, collectibility probable).
  2. Identify the performance obligations — distinct goods or services promised.
  3. Determine the transaction price, including variable consideration (change orders, incentives, penalties) constrained to amounts highly probable not to reverse.
  4. Allocate the transaction price to the performance obligations based on relative standalone selling prices.
  5. Recognize revenue when (point in time) or as (over time) each obligation is satisfied.

Over time versus a point in time

Revenue is recognized over time if any one criterion is met: the customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits; the entity creates or enhances an asset the customer controls; or the asset has no alternative use and the entity has an enforceable right to payment for work completed. A typical construction contract on the customer's land meets the over-time criteria. If none are met, revenue is recognized at a point in time (e.g., a spec home sold from inventory recognizes at closing when control transfers).

Measuring progress — cost-to-cost

For over-time recognition, progress is measured by an input or output method; construction commonly uses the cost-to-cost input method: percent complete = costs incurred to date ÷ total estimated costs. Illustrative contract: price $2,000,000, total estimated cost $1,600,000, costs incurred to date $800,000.

Percent complete = $800,000 ÷ $1,600,000 = 50%. Cumulative revenue = 50% × $2,000,000 = $1,000,000; cost of revenue $800,000; gross profit $200,000.

Contract assets and contract liabilities

Compare revenue recognized to amounts billed. With billings to date of $900,000 against recognized revenue of $1,000,000, the entity has under-billed by $100,000 — a contract asset (costs and estimated earnings in excess of billings) of $100,000. If instead billings were $1,150,000, the entity would have a contract liability (billings in excess of costs) of $150,000. This is exactly the over/under-billing schedule from CMA month 4 — FAR names the balance-sheet accounts contract asset and contract liability.

Estimate changes and losses

Changes in estimated cost or price are accounted for prospectively as a change in estimate — catch up the cumulative percent-complete in the current period, not by restating prior periods. But an expected loss on a contract is recognized immediately and in full as soon as it is anticipated, regardless of percent complete — the conservatism the CMA gross-profit-fade discussion warned about.

Transaction price, variable consideration, and the constraint

Step three — determining the transaction price — is where construction contracts get hard, because the price includes variable consideration: change orders, claims, performance bonuses, and liquidated-damages penalties. The entity estimates variable consideration using either the expected value (probability-weighted) or the most likely amount, whichever better predicts the outcome. Crucially, the estimate is subject to the constraint: include variable consideration only to the extent it is highly probable that a significant revenue reversal will not occur. An unapproved change order is therefore not booked at its full hoped-for value; it is constrained until approval makes the amount highly probable. The transaction price also reflects a significant financing component when payment timing gives one party a material financing benefit, and any noncash consideration is measured at fair value.

Contract modifications follow their own rules. A modification is treated as a separate contract if it adds distinct goods/services at their standalone price; otherwise it is accounted for prospectively (a termination-and-new-contract) or through a cumulative catch-up, depending on whether the remaining goods are distinct. Change orders on a single, integrated construction job typically fold into the existing performance obligation with a cumulative catch-up to percent-complete.

Principal versus agent, contract costs, and licenses

When another party is involved, the entity decides whether it is a principal (it controls the good/service before transfer — record revenue gross) or an agent (it arranges for another to provide it — record only the net commission). A general contractor that controls and is responsible for subcontracted work is generally a principal and reports the gross contract revenue, not just its markup.

ASC 340-40 governs contract costs: the incremental costs of obtaining a contract (a sales commission paid only on winning) are capitalized and amortized if recovery is expected, while costs of obtaining a contract that would have been incurred regardless are expensed. Costs to fulfill a contract are capitalized only if they relate directly to the contract, generate or enhance resources used to satisfy it, and are expected to be recovered. Finally, revenue from licenses of intellectual property is recognized either over time (a right to access IP that changes over the license period) or at a point in time (a right to use IP as it exists at grant) — a distinction the exam tests alongside the over-time-versus-point-in-time criteria for goods and services.

Presentation, disclosure, and the contract balances

ASC 606 also dictates presentation. Netting a contract's rights and obligations produces either a contract asset (revenue recognized ahead of the unconditional right to bill) or a contract liability (consideration received or due ahead of performance), shown separately from an unconditional receivable — a right to payment conditioned only on the passage of time. The distinction matters because a receivable is subject to credit-loss measurement while a contract asset carries both performance and credit risk, and a single contract is presented net rather than grossed up.

The standard's disclosure requirements are extensive: disaggregation of revenue into categories that depict how economic factors affect it; the opening and closing contract balances and the revenue recognized from prior-period contract liabilities; the remaining performance obligations (backlog) and when they will be recognized; and the significant judgments in applying the five steps, including how variable consideration and the constraint were estimated. For a contractor these disclosures surface the backlog and change-order judgments the face of the statements cannot show, which is exactly why a sophisticated reader looks to the notes first and why ASC 606 is as much a disclosure standard as a recognition one. The recognition and the disclosure travel together: a revenue number the notes cannot explain — with what judgments, against what backlog, under what constraint — is an incomplete answer to the question the standard was written to address.

CMA bridge

CMA month 4 built the WIP schedule and over/under-billings operationally; FAR formalizes it as ASC 606 with the five steps, the over-time criteria, and the contract-asset/contract-liability terminology. The $100,000 underbilling here is the same figure as the CMA flagship exemplar.

Practice and recap

  1. Apply the five steps in order.
  2. Test the three over-time criteria; otherwise recognize at a point in time.
  3. Measure progress with cost-to-cost and compute cumulative revenue.
  4. Classify under-billing as a contract asset and over-billing as a contract liability.
  5. Treat estimate changes prospectively but recognize anticipated losses immediately.

Recap: ASC 606's five steps recognize a construction contract's revenue over time by cost-to-cost; at 50% complete MBG's illustrative contract shows $1,000,000 revenue and a $100,000 contract asset — the WIP schedule from CMA month 4 expressed in FAR's language.

flashcards.front: The five steps of ASC 606 (in order)
flashcards.back: Identify the contract; identify performance obligations; determine the transaction price; allocate it; recognize revenue as/when obligations are satisfied.

flashcards.front: Three criteria for recognizing revenue OVER TIME
flashcards.back: Customer consumes as produced; entity creates/enhances an asset the customer controls; or no alternative use plus enforceable right to payment for work done.
Costs incurred to date ÷ total estimated costs.
Revenue recognized > billings = contract asset (underbilling); billings > revenue = contract liability (overbilling).

flashcards.front: How are changes in estimate handled?
flashcards.back: Prospectively (cumulative catch-up in the current period), not by restating prior periods.

flashcards.front: How is an anticipated contract loss recognized?
flashcards.back: Immediately and in full when anticipated, regardless of percent complete.

questions.q: Which is the correct order of the first three ASC 606 steps?
questions.explain: Step 1 identify the contract, step 2 identify performance obligations, step 3 determine the transaction price.

questions.q: Contract price $2,000,000, total estimated cost $1,600,000, costs to date $800,000. Percent complete (cost-to-cost) is:
At 50% complete on a $2,000,000 contract, cumulative revenue recognized is:
Revenue recognized is $1,000,000 and billings to date are $900,000. The balance sheet shows a:
questions.explain: Revenue exceeds billings by $100,000 — an underbilling, reported as a contract asset.

questions.q: Revenue is recognized OVER TIME when, among the criteria, the asset:
choices: Is always sold at a point in time
Has no alternative use and the entity has an enforceable right to payment for work completed
questions.explain: No-alternative-use plus an enforceable right to payment is one of the three over-time criteria.

questions.q: An anticipated loss on a contract is recognized:
choices: Immediately and in full when anticipated
questions.explain: Expected contract losses are recognized immediately and in full, regardless of percent complete.

questions.q: A change in the total estimated cost of a contract is accounted for:
choices: Prospectively as a change in estimate (cumulative catch-up)
questions.explain: Estimate changes are handled prospectively with a current-period cumulative catch-up.
